name: Jubilee Country Park
text: Your train passes near Jubilee Country Park, on the train's {side}, bought by Bromley Council to mark the Queen's Silver Jubilee in 1977 and opened as a park in 1981. A local nature reserve of grassland and ancient woodland, it has a large population of the rare corkyfruit water dropwort, and the London Loop walk runs through it.

name: The Daylight Inn
text: Your train passes near the Daylight Inn, on the train's {side}, a pub built at Petts Wood in 1935 for Charrington's Brewery. It is named after William Willett, who lived in Petts Wood and came up with the idea of daylight saving, and for many years old legal restrictions meant no other pub could be built within a mile of it.

name: Chislehurst Caves
text: Your train passes near Chislehurst Caves, on the train's {side}, some 22 miles of man-made tunnels and caverns dug as chalk and flint mines and first mentioned in a ninth-century Saxon charter. In the Second World War they became an air-raid shelter for up to 15,000 people, who paid a penny to go in, with electric lighting, a chapel and a hospital.

name: Elmstead Pit
text: Your train passes near Elmstead Pit, on the train's {side}, a small geological Site of Special Scientific Interest opposite Elmstead Woods station. It shows a layer of the Blackheath Beds laid down about 50 million years ago in an estuary, rich in fossils such as molluscs, sharks' teeth and fish scales; there is no public access.

name: Grove Park Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Grove Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1935 and listed in 2003 as a Grade II landscape of special historic interest for its carefully planned 1930s layout. It holds 56 Commonwealth war graves of the Second World War, with a memorial wall in the war graves plot at its centre.

name: Chinbrook Meadows
text: Your train passes near Chinbrook Meadows, on the train's {side}, a park of about half a mile from north to south on Lewisham's border with Bromley. The River Quaggy flows north through it, and both the Green Chain Walk and the Capital Ring cross it.

name: Bromley College
text: Your train passes near Bromley College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1666 under the will of John Warner, Bishop of Rochester, to house 20 widows of clergy. Its almshouses were built round a quadrangle in 1670 to 1672 and are the oldest building in Bromley, listed Grade I; it still provides homes for retired clergy and their families.

name: The Warren, Bromley
text: Your train passes near the Warren, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve at St Mary Cray managed by the London Wildlife Trust. It is mainly ancient oak and silver birch woodland, with bluebells and foxgloves, and a pond with plants rare in London such as blue fleabane and hare's-foot clover.

name: Orpington engine shed
text: Your train passes Orpington's former engine shed, beside the line just north of the station, where the main line's four tracks narrow to two at the end of the suburban belt. The steam depot had a 55-foot turntable; after electrification it closed and became offices for train drivers, and since 2007 it has held a training centre with a driving simulator.

name: Crofton Roman Villa
text: Your train passes near Crofton Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, beside Orpington station. Lived in from about AD 140 to 400 as the centre of a farming estate, it was found in 1926 by workmen making a drive for new council offices; the remains of ten rooms can be seen, with tiled floors and underfloor heating.

name: Hewitt's Chalk Bank
text: Your train passes near Hewitt's Chalk Bank, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve run by the Kent Wildlife Trust on a former refuse tip. Its large mound is the soil dug out when a railway tunnel was made, and its grassland has unusual plants such as grass vetchling and dark mullein.

name: The Paragon, Blackheath
text: Your train passes near the Paragon, on the train's {side}, a curved crescent of 14 large houses on the edge of the heath at Blackheath, designed by Michael Searles and begun in 1794. It is seven pairs of houses linked by six single-storey colonnades, said to use pillars from the demolished Wricklemarsh mansion, and it is listed Grade I.

name: Blackheath F.C.
text: Your train passes near the ground of Blackheath Football Club, on the train's {side}, a rugby union club founded in 1858 by old boys of Blackheath Proprietary School. It is the oldest open rugby club in continuous existence in the world, and helped to organise the first rugby international, between England and Scotland in 1871.

name: Well Hall
text: Your train passes near Well Hall, on the train's {side}, once a manor owned by William Roper and his wife Margaret, the daughter of Sir Thomas More. The Tudor Barn built for Roper in about 1525 beside the manor house still stands, with the moat, though the house itself was pulled down in the 1730s.

name: Shoulder of Mutton Green
text: Your train passes near Shoulder of Mutton Green, on the train's {side}, an open space at Welling beside the old London to Dover road, named for its triangular shape. In the Second World War it held a large public air-raid shelter, and part of its entrance can still be seen near the bus stop on Bellegrove Road.

name: Park View Road
text: Your train passes near Park View Road, on the train's {side}, the football ground at Welling, named after the stretch of road beside Danson Park, where Welling United have played since 1977. Football has been played there since the 1920s; Erith & Belvedere have shared the ground since 1999, after the main stand at their own ground burnt down.

name: Barnehurst railway station
text: Barnehurst station, at one end of this stretch, opened on May 1st 1895, when the Bexley Heath Railway opened its line from Blackheath to Slade Green. Its platforms sit just east of the bridge that carries Barnehurst Lane over the line.

name: St Augustine's Church, Slade Green
text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Church, Slade Green, on the train's {side}, founded in 1900 as a daughter church of St Paulinus in Crayford and a parish of its own from 1925. In the Second World War it sheltered families bombed out of east London; it was rebuilt after a direct hit in 1944, and again after a fire in 1991.

name: Erith Playhouse
text: Your train passes near Erith Playhouse, on the train's {side}, which opened as the Oxford Cinema on July 27th 1913, showing silent films. In the Second World War it stored furniture from bombed homes, and from 1947 the volunteers of Erith Theatre Guild spent two years turning it into a theatre, mostly in their spare time.

name: Erith Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Erith Town Hall, on the train's {side}, designed in the Italian Renaissance style by Harold Hind, the council's surveyor, and opened on June 2nd 1932. It replaced Walnut Tree House, the old house the council had moved into in 1902, and its pediment carries the town's coat of arms.

name: Lesnes Abbey
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Lesnes Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1178 for a small group of canons regular, on rising ground above what was once marshland. The ruins are a scheduled monument, and part of the woods beside them is a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest, important for fossils.

name: Crayford Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of Crayford Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound stadium that opened on September 1st 1986, built to replace the older Crayford & Bexleyheath Stadium beside it. Its last race meeting was held on January 19th 2025.

name: Slade Green Depot
text: Your train passes near Slade Green Depot, on the train's {side}, a railway depot on Crayford marshes whose brick shed of ten roads was finished on October 27th 1899, at first under the name Whitehall, Erith. Its budget allowed for building 145 houses for railway workers.

name: Hall Place
text: Your train passes near Hall Place, on the train's {side}, a house built in 1537 for Sir John Champneys, a merchant and former Lord Mayor of London, partly from stone taken from Lesnes Abbey. Its walls have a chequerboard pattern of flint and rubble, and a red-brick wing was added by Sir Robert Austen, who bought it in 1649; it is listed Grade I.

name: King's Head, Bexley
text: Your train passes near the King's Head, on the train's {side}, a pub on Bexley High Street in a building dating back to the 16th or early 17th century. It is listed Grade II.

name: Lamorbey Park
text: Your train passes near Lamorbey Park, on the train's {side}, a park set round Lamorbey House, a Grade II listed mansion. The estate's earliest recorded owner, in 1495, was a reeve named Thomas Sparrow, and a later owner was Charles FitzRoy, a son of Charles II; parts of it are now Rose Bruford College, two schools and a golf club, and its 1920s Glade has a large lake.

name: Metropolitan Police Museum
text: Your train passes near the Metropolitan Police Museum, on the train's {side}, at Marlowe House in Sidcup, where a new gallery opened in 2023. Its collection began with an appeal for objects in 1949, to mark 200 years since the Bow Street Runners, and was first kept at Bow Street police station.

name: The Tarn
text: Your train passes near the Tarn, on the train's {side}, a garden, bird sanctuary and lake among woodland between Mottingham and Eltham. The lake, once called Starbuck's Pond, was in the Great Park of Eltham Palace, a royal deer park until the Civil War; it opened as a garden in 1935 and has an 18th-century ice well.

name: Eltham College
text: Your train passes near Eltham College, on the train's {side}, a school founded in Victorian times for the sons and orphans of missionaries; David Livingstone sent his son Robert there in the 1850s. It moved here in 1912, to an 18th-century mansion called Fairy Hall that had been the Royal Naval School.

name: River Quaggy
text: Your train passes near the River Quaggy, on the train's {side}, which rises near Locksbottom and joins the River Ravensbourne near Lewisham station. In its upper reaches, through countryside near Chislehurst, it is known as the Kyd Brook.

name: Tower Hamlets Cemetery Park
text: Your train passes near Tower Hamlets Cemetery Park, on the train's {side}, one of London's Magnificent Seven Victorian cemeteries, opened in 1841 and known as Bow Cemetery. It closed in 1966 after 350,000 burials and is now a public park and local nature reserve, looked after by a friends' group.

name: Tower of London
text: Your train passes near the Tower of London, on the train's {side}, founded towards the end of 1066 as part of the Norman Conquest. Its White Tower was built by William the Conqueror, and over the centuries the Tower has been a royal palace, an armoury, a treasury, a menagerie and the home of the Royal Mint.

name: House Mill
text: Your train passes near the House Mill, on the train's {side}, a tide mill on the River Lea built in 1776 by Daniel Bisson and thought to be the largest tidal mill standing in Britain. Mills on this site are recorded in the Domesday Book, and much of its machinery survives, including four waterwheels; it is listed Grade I.

name: Memorial Grounds
text: Your train passes near the site of the Memorial Grounds, on the train's {side}, opened on Jubilee Day, June 22nd 1897, as the home of Thames Ironworks Football Club. The club played on there as West Ham United until it moved to the Boleyn Ground in 1904; the grounds also had a cycle track and one of England's largest open-air swimming pools.

name: London Sri Murugan Temple
text: Your train passes near London Sri Murugan Temple, on the train's {side}, a Hindu temple in Manor Park built of marble in the Dravidian style. Founded as a charity in 1975 and first consecrated in 1984, it gained its present building, with a temple tower 50 feet high, in 2005, and holds a chariot festival every August.

name: Woodgrange Park Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Woodgrange Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened on February 12th 1889 on land owned by the Marquess of Salisbury. The local MP objected to it in the House of Commons, as two other cemeteries were already close by.

name: Cart and Horses
text: Your train passes near the Cart and Horses, on the train's {side}, a pub at Maryland Point that moved here in about 1805. The heavy metal band Iron Maiden played here from 1976, with its founder Steve Harris, and a sign at the pub has called it the band's birthplace.

name: Theatre Royal Stratford East
text: Your train passes near Stratford East, once the Theatre Royal, on the train's {side}, a Victorian theatre that opened on December 17th 1884. From 1953 it was the home of Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop, which staged A Taste of Honey and Oh, What a Lovely War! there, and her statue stands outside.

name: Stratford Works
text: Your train passes near the site of Stratford Works, on the train's {side}, where the Great Eastern Railway built 1,702 locomotives. In 1891 the works built a complete tender engine in nine hours and 47 minutes, a record that still stands; the last of the works closed in 1991.

name: Manor Park Cemetery and Crematorium
text: Your train passes near Manor Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1874. Among those buried here are Jack Cornwell, who was given the Victoria Cross after his death, and Sarah Chapman, a leader of the matchgirls' strike of 1888 at Bryant & May.
